title: Opaque lane guard and preemptive queueing for tenant isolation
creator: Anika Rao
description:
Problem statement:
Customers on Dedicated report intermittent throughput drops when other tenants burst; current lane and quota systems are reactive and either throttle aggressively (hurting tail latency) or allow noisy neighbors to steal ephemeral capacity. We need a mechanism that preserves tenant separation guarantees and throughput contracts while allowing efficient bin-packing across GPUs.

Goals:
- Enforce soft isolation windows that protect committed throughput without full hard-slicing of GPUs.
- Provide a preemptive queueing layer to avoid sudden evictions; allow short, controlled queuing for low-latency requests.
- Add an opaque lane guard so scheduler decisions are made on lane metadata (capacity class) rather than tenant identifiers to reduce cross-tenant signal leakage and privacy surface.
- Integrate with autoscaling backstops: when preemptive queues exceed thresholds, trigger reserved burst allocation or scale-up signal to Dedicated.

Design overview (high level):
1) Opaque lane tagging: requests are annotated with lane-class: {guaranteed, burst, best-effort} and a small entropy token (opaque) generated by the assignment controller. Scheduler uses lane-class + token to make packing decisions; tokens rotate periodically to prevent long-lived affinity that causes noisy neighbor patterns.
2) Preemptive queue layer: each GPU process exposes a short in-memory queue (50-200ms target per request) where incoming tokens can wait rather than being immediately evicted. Queue length is bounded per-lane-class and per-tenant soft-credit.
3) Soft preemption tokens: long-running or large-batch jobs get preemption tokens; when a guaranteed request arrives, the allocator first attempts fast eviction via token handoff to free KV caches; if eviction latency is above threshold, new request is queued for up to N ms while an autoscale backstop decision is made.
4) Autoscale backstop integration: queue saturation metrics feed the autoscaler. Two signals: (a) short-term queue pressure triggers reserved-burst allocation (if tenant has unused burst credits), (b) sustained pressure triggers ephemeral scale-up with capacity placement policy to avoid noisy hardware.
5) Telemetry and safety nets: define SLO signals (token wait time, eviction rate, preempted-kv-loss), alert thresholds, and an automated fallback that flips to hard-slice for the affected tenant if guarantees repeatedly fail.

Trade-offs considered:
- Hard-slicing (one-tenant-per-GPU) eliminates noisy neighbors but is wasteful. The proposed approach trades a small increase in scheduling complexity for much better utilization.
- Opaque tokens reduce per-tenant telemetry richness; we will emit tenant-level aggregates to billing and support but keep scheduling surface opaque to runtime to reduce cross-tenant coupling.
- Queuing adds tail latency vs immediate greedy admission; we constrain queues to sub-200ms so most interactive workloads see acceptable latency and autoscale handles the rest.

Implementation plan (rough milestones):
- Week 1-2: Allocator + token generation service (controller) prototype; add lane-class header to request path.
- Week 3-4: Scheduler support for token-based packing and opaque token rotation policy. Unit tests and integration harness.
- Week 5: In-process preemptive queue and soft preemption token handoff APIs. Local sim/harness to model eviction latency distributions.
- Week 6: Autoscale backstop hooks and metrics (Prometheus) + dashboard in Console.
- Week 7: Canary rollout to internal tenants in staging; monitor SLOs.
- Week 8-9: Gradual canary to small set of external Dedicated customers, gated by SLOs and opt-in.

Observability and dashboards:
- New metrics: lane_queue_wait_ms (p90/p99), preemption_eviction_ms, burst_credit_consumption, kernel_eviction_count, tenant_isolation_score.
- Console dashboard with per-tenant aggregates, per-GPU lane distribution heatmap, and an incidents time-series.
- Debug traces linked to GitHub PRs and Confluence runbooks.

Testing strategy:
- Unit: allocator heuristics, token rotation correctness, queue invariants.
- Integration: emulator with synthetic noisy neighbor patterns (spike generator), measure throughput and tail latency for guaranteed tenants.
- Chaos: simulate GPU slowdowns and forced KV cache eviction to validate fallback.

Rollout and rollback plan:
- Feature flagged at runtime per Dedicated fleet. Default off for all customers.
- Start with internal canary tenants on non-critical fleets. Promote to select tenants with small committed throughput.
- If SLA regressions observed (p95 latency increase > 15% for guaranteed lanes, or queue_wait_ms p99 > 300ms), automatically disable preemptive queueing for that tenant and force hard-slice fallback for 30 minutes while engineers investigate.

Open questions and decisions needed:
- Burst credit accounting: should reserved burst be per-region or global per-customer? (recommend per-region to reduce cross-region capacity churn).
- Token rotation frequency trade-off: shorter rotation reduces affinity but increases churn. Empirically tune.
- How to expose telemetry to customers without exposing opaque token internals? propose aggregate metrics and billing-only detailed logs on request.

Links and artifacts:
- Confluence spec (draft): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Opaque+Lane+Guard+Design
- Scheduler prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2801
- Autoscale hooks draft: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zExampleAutoscaleBackstop
- Evaluation harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/test-harness/tree/opaque-queue

Expected outcomes:
- Preserve throughput guarantees for guaranteed-class tenants during common noisy bursts.
- Reduce emergency evictions by >40% in synthetic noisy-neighbor tests while keeping utilization within 10% of current levels.
- Provide smoother path toward autoscale-driven capacity increases only when necessary, reducing overprovisioning.
